title: Kentucky's 4th Congressional District General Election, 2026
description: Kentucky's 4th Congressional District stretches across the northern part of the state, including the suburbs of Cincinnati, Covington, Newport, and rural counties along the Ohio River. The seat became open after seven-term Republican incumbent Thomas Massie was defeated in the May 19, 2026 Republican primary by former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump in what became the most expensive House primary in U.S. history. Gallrein faces Democrat Melissa Strange, a supply chain director and first-time candidate, along with Libertarian Jeremy Todd and Kentucky Party candidate Mohammad Ahmad in the general election. The district has a Cook Partisan Voting Index of R+18 and has not elected a Democrat since 2004, making Gallrein the heavy favorite in this solidly Republican seat.
polling_note: No general election polls have been conducted yet for this race as of mid-2026. The Republican primary (May 19, 2026) polls showed Gallrein leading Massie, with final results of 54.9% to 45.1%.

candidates.name: Ed Gallrein
candidates.summary: Ed Gallrein is a retired Navy SEAL officer and fifth-generation Kentucky dairy farmer who defeated seven-term incumbent Thomas Massie in the Republican primary with President Donald Trump's endorsement. He served 30 years in the U.S. Navy including deployments to Panama, Afghanistan, Iraq, and the Persian Gulf, retiring with the rank of Captain after serving with SEAL Team Six. Gallrein campaigns on supporting Trump's agenda, cutting taxes and regulations, securing the border, and reducing government spending.

candidates.name: Melissa Strange
candidates.summary: Melissa Strange is a supply chain director with 27 years of experience in the food manufacturing and agribusiness industry, making her first run for elected office. She holds a bachelor's degree in International Studies from Northern Kentucky University and an MBA from Thomas More University, and has volunteered as an academic team coach for 16 years. Strange campaigns on rebuilding the economy for working families, expanding access to healthcare and reproductive rights, and investing in public education and Pre-K for All.

candidates.name: Jeremy Todd
candidates.summary: Jeremy Todd is the Libertarian Party candidate for Kentucky's 4th Congressional District, a Northern Kentucky resident who secured ballot access by gathering over 750 signatures in 12 days. He campaigns on an anti-war, anti-spending, and anti-establishment platform, emphasizing bringing U.S. troops home, cutting government spending and the national debt, and opposing influence of special interests and foreign lobbies. Todd's candidacy has attracted support from some of former Congressman Thomas Massie's allies following Massie's primary defeat.

candidates.name: Mohammad Ahmad
candidates.summary: Mohammad Ahmad is the Kentucky Party candidate for Kentucky's 4th Congressional District, a Covington resident and Palestinian-American activist who previously led the Ceasefire Now Covington Coalition. He is a vocal critic of U.S. military intervention abroad and Zionism, and the Kentucky Party opposes the use of military force and advocates ending Kentucky's participation in overseas interventions. Ahmad campaigns on putting 'America first means Israel last,' eliminating foreign manipulation in elections, and prioritizing community building in the Bluegrass region.

forecast.rationale: No general-election polls exist for this race, so the forecast relies entirely on structural factors. Kentucky's 4th District carries a Cook PVI of R+18 and has not elected a Democrat to Congress since 2004, giving it one of the strongest Republican baselines in the country. The seat is open following incumbent Thomas Massie's primary loss, which introduces some uncertainty — but the Republican nominee, Ed Gallrein, emerged from a high-turnout, heavily funded primary with Donald Trump's endorsement and a decisive 54.9% victory. The Democratic candidate, Melissa Strange, is a credible first-time candidate but faces an extremely uphill climb in a district where Democrats have not been competitive at the federal level for over two decades. The Libertarian and Kentucky Party candidates could attract a modest protest vote but are not expected to alter the overall outcome. The absence of any general-election polling tempers confidence to medium, but the district's underlying partisanship and historical voting patterns point to an overwhelming Republican advantage.
